resources.string: Training load is calculated from heart rate and needs your maximum and resting heart rate.
No training yet. Workouts with heart rate appear here after the next sync.

# Daily load
The stress scores of the day's workouts added up; an hour at threshold heart rate scores 100. Walks and rides that an app detected by itself are left out.

# Fitness and fatigue
- Fitness: daily load averaged over about six weeks (a 42-day exponential average). It rises slowly with consistent training.
- Fatigue: the same over about a week. It reacts to the last few sessions.

# Form
Yesterday's fitness minus yesterday's fatigue: how fresh you are going into the day.
- Negative while you build fitness.
- Positive when you ease off, for example in the days before a race.
- It only knows your training. Sleep, illness and stress are covered by readiness on Today.

# Reading the chart
- Ramp rate is the change in fitness over the last seven days.
- Touch the chart and slide along it to read any day.

Weeks run from Monday to Sunday.

- Load: the stress scores of the week added up.
- Hours: the duration of every workout that counts as training.
- Intensity: how the time with heart rate splits over your five zones, as on the session pages, or over the three of the intensity focus: below the first ventilatory threshold (VT1), between VT1 and VT2, and above VT2. The switch under the table picks one. The two do not nest exactly: the threshold zone straddles VT2.

Studies of successful endurance athletes typically find most of their training time, often around 80 %, below VT1 (Seiler 2010).

# The shaded band
The load that builds fitness without a jump: from 0.8 to 1.3 times a usual week at the fitness the week started with (7 x fitness). Below it fitness falls; above it the week is a jump the body is not used to. This is the acute to chronic workload ratio's sweet spot (Gabbett 2016); its use for injury prediction is disputed (Impellizzeri 2020), so it is a guide, not a target to hit.
Nightly HRV with its seven-day average and normal range
Nightly resting heart rate with its seven-day average and usual range

How your body handles training over weeks and months, measured each night.

# Reading the charts
- Dots are single nights, the line is the average of the last seven days.
- The shaded band is your own normal range on each day, the same one readiness uses; it moves as your baseline does.
- The line turns orange while the week sits outside the band.

# HRV
The normal range is the mean of the last 60 days, plus or minus half a standard deviation, on the log scale (Plews 2013). A week below the range is the clearest sign of accumulated fatigue, illness or stress; a rising range over months often comes with better fitness.

The 7-day variation is the coefficient of variation of ln HRV over the week (Plews 2012; HRV4Training shows it the same way), with your usual range from the previous 60 days. A steady mean with rising variation points to a disturbed balance: hard training, illness or travel. In elite triathletes a falling mean with shrinking variation came before non-functional overreaching (Plews 2012), so read it together with the mean.

# Resting heart rate
The usual range is the average of the last 30 nights, plus or minus one standard deviation, at least 3 bpm. A raised resting heart rate for several nights points the same way as low HRV.

Both need a week of nights before a range appears.

Load, VO2max and HRV in one word, with the reasons
Four weeks of time below, between and above the thresholds
Not enough training yet: the status needs four weeks of load and a fitness of at least 10.

One word for where training stands, from three measures, each with a fixed rule:

- Load: fatigue (the last week's load) over fitness (the last six weeks'), the exponentially weighted acute to chronic load ratio. 0.8 to 1.5 is your usual training; above 1.5 is a jump the body rarely absorbs for long (Gabbett 2016); below 0.8 is a lighter week.
- VO2max: the change of the VO2max trend over four weeks. Half a ml/kg/min or more either way counts as rising or falling.
- HRV: the week's HRV against its normal range, as readiness judges it.

# The rules, in order
- HRV below its normal range while training: strained.
- Load ratio above 1.5: overreaching.
- Load ratio below 0.5 and fitness falling over two weeks: detraining.
- Load ratio below 0.8: peaking when you are fresh, fitness is within 10 % of its 90-day high and VO2max is not falling; otherwise recovery.
- Otherwise by VO2max: rising productive, falling unproductive, steady maintaining.

The words are Garmin's, whose own rules are not published; these are PacingLab's, built from the same ingredients.
Too little running or riding in the last four weeks to tell.
Balanced: every zone within its target

How the last four weeks of running and riding split over the three intensity zones, by time with heart rate, against target bands. Garmin's load focus shows the same idea with bands it does not publish; these come from the training of successful endurance athletes, which is pyramidal or polarized (Seiler 2010; Stöggl and Sperlich 2015; Kenneally 2018):

- Below VT1: 70 to 90 %. Easy running builds the aerobic base and is what allows the hard sessions.
- VT1 to VT2: up to 25 %. Tempo and threshold work; more than this tends to stall progress in trained athletes.
- Above VT2: 5 to 20 %. Intervals at or above threshold.

The distribution's shape follows Treff (2019): polarized when zone 1 > zone 3 > zone 2 with a polarization index above 2, pyramidal when zone 1 > zone 2 > zone 3, threshold-focused or high-intensity when zone 2 or zone 3 is the largest.

Heart rate lags at the start of each rep, so short reps count partly in a lower zone. Gym sessions and other sports are left out.

resources.string: How far you ran this week against what your legs are used to: the average of the four weeks before plus 30 % (Settings > Training can make it 20 or 10 %). Bars are weeks (Monday to Sunday); the tick over each bar is that week\'s tolerance; a week above it turns orange.\n\nRunners who raised their weekly distance by more than 30 % had more overuse injuries (knee, iliotibial band) than those who stayed within 10 % (Nielsen 2014), and in half-marathon training, increases of 20 to 60 % came with more injuries in the first weeks (Damsted 2019). The evidence is limited, so read it as a caution, not a limit: a big week after a quiet month is the case to watch. Garmin\'s running tolerance rests on the same idea with its own, unpublished rule; it also counts hills and running form, which a Sense does not measure.

A dot on each day with training. Its area grows with the day's load (the largest dot is the biggest day of the last six months); its colour is the goal of the day's hardest session, in the zone colours of the intensity focus (Seiler 2010 names sessions by their goal: an interval day counts as hard although most of its minutes are easy).

- Runs take the kind their session page names: easy and long runs below VT1, tempo and threshold work between the thresholds, VO2max intervals and sprints above VT2. A threshold session counts as threshold work even when its heart rate crossed VT2 for a while.
- Other runs and rides go by heart rate: above VT2 from 15 %% of the time, between the thresholds from 20 %%, otherwise below VT1.
- Grey days had only other training, such as gym sessions or walks, or no heart rate: zones describe running and riding, not lifting.

Tap a day to open its main session.

# Load
With heart rate $\mathrm{HR}_t$ sampled through a workout, its share of the heart rate reserve is

$$x_t = \frac{\mathrm{HR}_t - \mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{rest}}}{\mathrm{HR}_{\max} - \mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{rest}}}$$

clamped to 0 to 1. Banister's training impulse (1991), with $\Delta t$ in minutes (gaps count at most 15 seconds):

$$\mathrm{TRIMP} = \sum_t \Delta t\; x_t\, a\, e^{b\, x_t}$$

with $a = 0.64$, $b = 1.92$ for men and $a = 0.86$, $b = 1.67$ for women. The stress score sets one hour at threshold heart rate, $x_{\mathrm{LT}}$, to 100:

$$\mathrm{SS} = 100\, \frac{\mathrm{TRIMP}}{60\, x_{\mathrm{LT}}\, a\, e^{b\, x_{\mathrm{LT}}}}$$

The daily load $L_d$ is the sum of the day's stress scores.

# Fitness, fatigue and form
Fitness $C$ and fatigue $A$ are exponential averages with time constants of 42 and 7 days:

$$k_\tau = 1 - e^{-1/\tau}$$

$$C_d = C_{d-1} + k_{42}\, (L_d - C_{d-1})$$

$$A_d = A_{d-1} + k_{7}\, (L_d - A_{d-1})$$

Both start at the mean daily load of the first 42 days. Form is how fresh you are going into the day, and the ramp rate the change in fitness over a week:

$$T_d = C_{d-1} - A_{d-1}$$

$$\mathrm{ramp}_d = C_d - C_{d-7}$$

With fitness $C$ on the Sunday before the week, a usual week's load is $7C$ and the shaded band

$$B = \left[\,0.8 \cdot 7C,\;\; 1.3 \cdot 7C\,\right]$$

which is an acute to chronic load ratio between 0.8 and 1.3 (Gabbett 2016). No band is drawn while $C < 5$.

Each intensity column is the share of the week's time with heart rate spent in that zone:

$$p_k = \frac{t_k}{\sum_j t_j}$$

# HRV
The line is the geometric mean of the last seven days (at least 3 nights), with $h = \ln \mathrm{RMSSD}$:

$$\bar{h}_7 = \frac{1}{n_7} \sum_{d} h_d, \quad \mathrm{line} = e^{\bar{h}_7}$$

The band on each day comes from the 60 days up to it (at least 7 nights), with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $s$:

$$e^{\mu - s/2} \;\text{ to }\; e^{\mu + s/2}$$

The 7-day variation is the coefficient of variation of $h$ over the week (at least 5 nights), in per cent:

$$\mathrm{CV}_7 = 100\, \frac{\operatorname{sd}(h)}{\bar{h}}$$

with its usual range the 10th to 90th percentile of the weekly values of the previous 60 days (at least 14 of them).

# Resting heart rate
Over the last 30 nights, with mean $\bar{r}$ and standard deviation $s_r$:

$$\bar{r} \pm \max(s_r,\; 3\,\mathrm{bpm})$$

Over the last 28 days of runs and rides, the share of time with heart rate in each domain:

$$z_k = \frac{t_k}{t_1 + t_2 + t_3}$$

Treff's polarization index (2019), with $z_2$ at least 0.01:

$$\mathrm{PI} = \log_{10}\left(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\, z_3 \cdot 100\right)$$

- Threshold: $z_2$ the largest.
- High intensity: $z_3$ the largest.
- Polarized: $z_1$ the largest, $z_3 > z_2$ and $\mathrm{PI} > 2$.
- Pyramidal: $z_1$ the largest and $z_2 \ge z_3$.

At least 2 hours of endurance training are needed.

With $D_w$ the distance run in week $w$, the usual week is the mean of the four weeks before, and the tolerance adds the chosen increase $p$ (30 % unless changed in Settings):

$$\bar{D}_w = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{k=1}^{4} D_{w-k}$$

$$T_w = (1 + p)\, \bar{D}_w$$

A week is above its tolerance when $D_w > T_w$. Without running in the four weeks before there is no tolerance.

How much higher your heart rate ran than usual while you were still and awake: heart rate that movement does not explain. Physiologists call it additional heart rate and use it as a sign of emotional strain in daily life (Myrtek 2004). It is not a measure of how stressed you feel, and a watch cannot see cortisol.

# How it is worked out
- Still minutes: no steps on any device in that minute or the 5 before, not in bed, not during a workout or the hour after it (15 minutes after a detected walk or ride), and heart rate at most 130.
- Your usual: for each hour of the day, the median heart rate of your still minutes over the four weeks before, so that your daily rhythm and habits such as sitting at work are taken out.
- The day: how far its still minutes ran above those hourly usuals, in bpm, from two hours of still time.
- The score: 50 is a usual day for you, and every 10 points is one typical day-to-day spread above or below. Calm below 40, usual to 60, raised from 60, high from 70.
- Today counts so far and is read again every few minutes while the app is open.

# How far to trust it
Confidence is low to moderate, so it is marked experimental:
- In daily life, wrist heart rate measures explain only a few per cent of how stressed people say they feel (1 to 3 % in 657 people over eight weeks; JMIR Cardio 2021). In the lab, heart rate corrected for movement told mental from physical stress apart only weakly (van de Ven 2025).
- Much besides stress raises still heart rate: illness, heat, caffeine, alcohol the night before, a large meal, dehydration, short sleep, hard training and standing rather than sitting, which the watch cannot see. A ride without steps is left out only when an app detected it or heart rate went above 130.
- It describes your body, not your mind: a raised day means something put a load on it. Where your data shows one, the card names it: vitals off around that day (often an illness starting), hard training or a poor night.

# What it is good for
Spotting days and weeks when your body runs hotter than usual, and a factor in Sleep factors. Single days are noisy; a run of raised days says more.

It needs about three weeks of wearing the watch in the day: one for the hourly usuals, two more to set the scale.

# Still minutes
A minute $m$ is still when it has at least 3 heart rate samples, no steps from $m - 5$ to $m$, lies outside sleep records and workouts (from 5 minutes before to 60 after, or 15 after a detected walk or ride), and its mean heart rate $h_m \le 130$.

# Hourly usual
For hour $k$ of day $d$, with $\bar{h}_{k,d'}$ the mean still heart rate of hour $k$ on an earlier day $d'$ (with at least 10 still minutes in that hour), from at least 7 days:

$$u_{k,d} = \operatorname*{median}_{d - 28 \le d' < d} \bar{h}_{k,d'}$$

# Excess
With $n_{k,d}$ the still minutes of hour $k$, over the hours that have a usual and from 120 still minutes:

$$E_d = \frac{\sum_k n_{k,d}\, \left(\bar{h}_{k,d} - u_{k,d}\right)}{\sum_k n_{k,d}}$$

# Score
With $\tilde{E}$ the median of $E$ over the 28 days before and MAD its median absolute deviation (at least 14 days):

$$s = \max\left(1.4826\, \mathrm{MAD},\; 1.5\right)$$

$$S_d = 50 + 10\, \frac{E_d - \tilde{E}}{s}$$

clamped to 0 to 100: a T-score among your own days, made robust to odd days by the median and MAD.

# Other causes
- Vitals: two or more of HRV, resting heart rate, breathing rate, SpO2 and skin temperature outside their usual range on the morning of the day or the next.
- Hard training: a day's load $L_d \ge 60$ and $L_d \ge 1.5\, C_{d-1}$, with $C$ fitness, that day or the day before.
- Poor sleep: a sleep score under 65 the night before.
Still heart rate against your usual, each day
It compares each day with your own usual days, so it needs three weeks of wearing the watch in the day.
